rules.name: Java 7 diamond operator for generic instance creation
rules.description: A generic constructor call spells out its type arguments explicitly (new HashMap<String, Object>()). Java 7 infers them from the assignment context, so the argument list can be replaced by the empty diamond <>. The pattern matches a 'new' expression carrying a non-empty type-argument list immediately before its constructor parentheses.

patterns.reason: Java 7 introduced type inference for generic instance creation: the explicit type arguments of a constructor call may be replaced by <> when the compiler can infer them from context.

rules.verification_hint: After the fix the right-hand side reads new X<>(...) while the declared type on the left is byte-identical to before. javac -source 1.7 must compile with no 'cannot infer type arguments' error.

blast_class_evidence.reasoning: The edit rewrites only the type-argument list of a constructor call on the right-hand side of an initializer or an argument expression. The declared type of the field/local on the left, every method signature, and every implements/extends clause stay byte-identical, so no other compilation unit is forced to change. Confirmed on the previous run: all 39 applied DIAMOND_OPERATOR diffs touched only the RHS expression.

sites.what_changes: Field initializer: 'private List<CounterInfo> monitoredCounters = new ArrayList<CounterInfo>()' loses only the constructor's type arguments; the field's declared type List<CounterInfo> is untouched, so every reader of the field elsewhere keeps compiling.

Local variable initializer inside a private static method: only 'new HashMap<String, AverageMeasure>()' is erased to 'new HashMap<>()'; the local's declared type and the enclosing method signature do not move.

rules.name: Java 7 String in switch — if/else-if chain over String constants
rules.description: A branch of an if / else-if chain tests a String-valued expression against a string literal with .equals(). Java 7 permits String in a switch selector, so a chain of such branches over one receiver collapses into a switch with case labels. The pattern deliberately matches only the 'else if' head of a branch (so a lone, unchained if is never flagged), requires a string-literal argument (so an .equals() against an arbitrary object is never flagged), and rejects a negated condition.

patterns.reason: Java 7 added String support in the switch selector. Only an else-if branch comparing a String against a compile-time string constant is convertible to a case label; the previous run's broad '\.equals\s*\(\s*"' pattern flagged 121 sites of which 117 were single, unchained ifs and had to be SKIPPED.

rules.verification_hint: After the fix the chain is a single switch on the same receiver, every former branch body is preserved verbatim under its case label, no 'break;' follows an unconditional 'return', and the else-fallthrough becomes 'default'. javac must report no unreachable statement.

blast_class_evidence.reasoning: Every flagged branch sits inside a method or an anonymous-listener body and is rewritten into a switch in the same body. No field type, parameter type, return type or throws clause is part of the edit, so no caller has to change.

sites.what_changes: Five-branch chain (lines 276-297) over the local String 'command' inside an ActionListener body; it becomes 'switch (command) { case "Reset": ... }'. The listener's actionPerformed(ActionEvent) signature is outside the edit.
Same five-label shape (lines 295-313) over 'command'; each branch body (dlg.dispose(), retVal assignments) moves verbatim under a case label, and nothing outside the method body is touched.

counterexamples.reason: The preceding branch tests ((param = msg.getProtocol()) == null), not a String equals, and this condition is a disjunction with equalsIgnoreCase, so no switch case label can express it.
The preceding branch is if(!((Boolean) r.getParamAt(0)).booleanValue()), a boolean test, not a String equals, so this else-if is a lone String comparison and not a convertible chain.

rules.name: Java 7 try-with-resources — manually released external resource
rules.description: An external auto-closeable resource is acquired at this line: a java.io file stream/reader/writer, a java.net socket, a java.util.zip / java.util.jar archive, or a java.sql Statement/ResultSet. Pre-Java-7 code has to release it itself with an explicit close(), normally in a finally block, or it leaks; Java 7 try-with-resources closes it automatically when the block exits. The pattern flags the acquisition site - the line a conversion has to move into the try header - whether the resource is bound to a local variable or created inline as a call argument. In-memory streams (ByteArrayInputStream/OutputStream, StringReader/Writer), whose close() is a documented no-op and which are never a try-with-resources target, are deliberately excluded, as are cached java.sql PreparedStatement fields. An acquisition whose resource is stored in a field, and therefore deliberately outlives the method, is NOT this construct.

patterns.reason: Acquisition of an external java.io / java.net / java.util.zip resource via its constructor. Every listed type implements java.io.Closeable, which Java 7 retrofitted onto java.lang.AutoCloseable, so each is usable as a try-with-resources resource.

Local java.sql Statement / PreparedStatement / ResultSet declaration. Java 7 retrofitted java.sql.Statement and ResultSet to implement AutoCloseable. The leading negative lookahead drops field declarations (private/public/protected/static/final), which are cached for the object's lifetime and are not try-with-resources candidates.

rules.verification_hint: After the fix the resource is declared inside the try's parentheses, the manual close() call is gone, and any nested try/catch that existed only to swallow that close()'s exception is either removed (when the enclosing catch already covers it) or preserved explicitly. javac -source 1.7 must accept the resource type, which proves it implements AutoCloseable.

blast_class_evidence.reasoning: The conversion moves a local declaration into the try header of the same method body and deletes the matching close() statement. No signature, field type or import changes; the recipe's own invariants forbid a signature edit. The one behavioural risk (a previously swallowed close() exception now propagating) is confined to the same method, which is why the recipe is mode: agent and reports NEEDS_REVIEW instead of guessing.

sites.what_changes: 'FileWriter f = new FileWriter(fileName); BufferedWriter bw = new BufferedWriter(f);' (lines 374-375) move into the try header; the manual 'bw.close(); f.close();' at lines 392-393 disappears. The enclosing method body is the whole blast radius.

'InputStream in = new FileInputStream(storage);' inside load(String) becomes the try's resource; 'in.close();' at line 127 is dropped. The public 'void load(String storage) throws IOException' signature is unchanged.

counterexamples.reason: sc is the field 'protected Socket sc' declared at JICPConnection.java:58; the socket is owned by the connection object and closed in its own close() method, so it deliberately outlives this method.
HTTPServer.java:103 sits inside the /*#PJAVA_INCLUDE_BEGIN ... #PJAVA_INCLUDE_END*/ block comment; java_source.is_live_code() returns False for this line, so it is not compiled code at all.
The socket's stream is stored in the field 'private DataInputStream in' (line 59), so the socket must stay open after this method returns and cannot be scoped to a try-with-resources block here.
